anchorClaim: Individuals with eating disorders (anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, or clinical risk populations) show measurable structural or functional brain differences, in regions associated with emotion processing and cognitive control, detectable via MRI or fMRI compared to healthy controls.
confidenceSummary: This 35% score is Preliminary because nearly half of the 91 sources were flagged as a weak topic match, and manual checking found many describe unrelated conditions rather than eating disorders specifically, so the underlying evidence base is thinner than the raw source count suggests.
dataQualityNote: This file was fully rebuilt from verified production DynamoDB data (Datomers table record 65ba2769-243e-444b-8ee5-59c0f8ada7c2 and all 91 linked records in the datoms table, fetched via a single BatchGetItem call with zero unprocessed keys) after an earlier version was found to contain 12 fabricated datom entries whose claim, source, population, and methodology text did not match the live database (9 of those 12 records were not even about eating disorders in the live data). Every datom below and every aggregate figure was independently re-derived from the live records; none of the prior file's per-datom text was reused. Real data quality caveats surfaced in this rebuild: 44 of 91 datoms (48%) are flagged theme_match_low_confidence by the platform's own matching pipeline, and manual review shows about 34 of those are genuinely off topic (atopic dermatitis, tobacco use disorder, ADHD, borderline personality disorder, mind wandering EEG, and rodent studies) rather than direct eating disorder neuroimaging evidence. 40 of 91 datoms (44%) are evidence_type TEXT_NO_METADATA rather than PDF_FULL_TEXT, and 24 of 91 (26%) have sample_size recorded exactly as Not reported. The 91 datoms trace back to only 40 distinct source papers, with one Mendelian randomization study alone contributing 6. All 91 methodology fields are populated in the live data (no Not reported methodology values were found, unlike the prior file). No malformed or missing records were encountered.

datoms.claim: Individuals with anorexia nervosa show measurable structural brain differences in the striatum (putamen) detectable via MRI compared to healthy controls and other eating disorder subgroups.
datoms.source: R. Molina-Ruiz, J. Looi, M. Walterfang, T. García-Saiz, Fiona A. Wilkes "Striatal volumes as potential biomarkers in Eating Disorders: A pilot study." (2022). doi:10.1016/j.rpsmen.2022.06.003

datoms.measure: Left putaminal volume (striatal structural volume)
datoms.methodology: Cross-sectional MRI volumetric study
datoms.sample_size: 24 female patients plus 19 healthy controls (43 total)
datoms.notes: Limitations: Pilot study with small sample size; preliminary results requiring replication in larger cohorts.

datoms.claim: Individuals with anorexia nervosa show increased grey matter volume in the orbitofrontal cortex and medial temporal lobe compared to healthy controls, detectable via structural MRI.

datoms.measure: Grey matter volume in orbitofrontal cortex and medial temporal lobe
datoms.methodology: Meta-analysis of structural MRI studies
datoms.notes: Limitations: The meta-analysis was limited to structural MRI studies; functional neuroimaging data were not included in this analysis.

datoms.claim: Adult individuals with anorexia nervosa show structural brain differences in the genu of the anterior cingulate cortex compared to healthy controls, detectable via structural MRI.
datoms.source: Michelle Sader, Justin H. G. Williams, G. Waiter "A meta‐analytic investigation of grey matter differences in anorexia nervosa and autism spectrum disorder" (2022). doi:10.1002/erv.2915

datoms.measure: Structural differences in genu of anterior cingulate cortex
datoms.methodology: Meta-analysis of structural MRI studies
datoms.notes: Limitations: The meta-analysis was limited to structural MRI studies; functional neuroimaging data were not included in this analysis.

datoms.claim: Individuals with anorexia nervosa show measurable gray matter alterations in brain regions associated with the auditory network, default mode network, and sensorimotor network, detectable via structural MRI compared to healthy controls.
datoms.source: Hucheng Yang, Shu Wang, HuaLiang Li, Siyu Gu, Fengmei Zhang "Mapping gray matter changes in anorexia nervosa: a functional connectivity network approach" (2025). doi:10.3389/fnut.2025.1667729
datoms.population: 667 individuals with anorexia nervosa and 659 healthy controls from 26 studies
datoms.measure: Gray matter alterations mapped to functional brain networks via functional connectivity
datoms.methodology: Systematic review with functional connectivity network mapping
datoms.notes: Limitations: The study integrated data from multiple VBM studies with varying methodological quality and thresholds. The FCNM approach relies on mapping coordinates from prior studies onto functional connectivity data from healthy controls, which may not fully capture disease-specific functional alterations.

datoms.claim: Individuals with anorexia nervosa show measurable structural brain differences in the prefrontal cortex, nucleus accumbens, hippocampus, and insula compared to healthy controls, detectable via structural MRI.
datoms.source: M. Wayda-Zalewska, Agnieszka Pluta, Tomasz Wolak, Mateusz Wojtczak, Jakub Wojciechowski "Interaction between emotion lability, emotion regulation and structural brain abnormalities in patients with anorexia nervosa and borderline personality disorder" (2025). doi:10.3389/fnins.2025.1545599

datoms.measure: Gray matter volume and cortical thickness in prefrontal cortex, nucleus accumbens, hippocampus, insula
datoms.methodology: Structural MRI with volumetric and cortical thickness analysis
datoms.notes: Limitations: Study included only female subjects due to higher prevalence of AN diagnoses and unavailability of male patients. AN-Binge Eating/Purging Type patients were excluded. Cross-sectional design limits causal inference.

datoms.claim: Individuals with bulimia nervosa show increased gray matter volume in the left medial orbitofrontal cortex compared to healthy controls, detectable via structural MRI.
datoms.source: Weihua Li, Li-rong Tang, Miao Wang, Jiani Wang, T. Guo "Altered gray matter volume and functional connectivity in medial orbitofrontal cortex of bulimia nervosa patients: A combined VBM and FC study" (2022). doi:10.3389/fpsyt.2022.963092

datoms.measure: Gray matter volume in left medial orbitofrontal cortex
datoms.methodology: Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) structural MRI
datoms.notes: Limitations: Modest sample size limited to adult women, so results cannot be generalized to men. Single seed region selected for rsFC analysis. Descriptive rather than mechanistic study. Menstrual status not controlled.

datoms.claim: Individuals with anorexia nervosa show measurable gray matter volume reduction in brain regions compared to healthy controls, detectable via MRI.
datoms.source: Huaze Gao, Shuoyu Chen, Lei Wang, P. B. Shih "The Impact of Age on Gray Matter Volume Reduction in Anorexia Nervosa: A Systematic Review" (2025). doi:10.1101/2025.03.03.25322748

datoms.measure: Gray matter volume reduction detected via MRI
datoms.methodology: Systematic review and meta-analysis
datoms.notes: Limitations: The paper does not explicitly state limitations but notes greater variability in regional findings for older AN patients, suggesting heterogeneity in aging effects.

datoms.claim: Individuals with anorexia nervosa show measurable volume alterations in brain regions associated with emotion processing (hippocampus, amygdala) and cognitive control (precuneus), detectable via MRI compared to healthy controls.
datoms.source: Huaze Gao, Shuoyu Chen, Lei Wang, P. B. Shih "The Impact of Age on Gray Matter Volume Reduction in Anorexia Nervosa: A Systematic Review" (2025). doi:10.1101/2025.03.03.25322748

datoms.measure: Regional gray matter volume alterations in emotion processing and cognitive control regions via MRI
datoms.methodology: Systematic review and meta-analysis
datoms.notes: Limitations: The review notes greater variability in regional findings for older AN patients, which may limit generalizability of regional findings across age groups.

datoms.notes: Limitations: Not reported in the provided text.

datoms.claim: Females with atypical anorexia nervosa show significantly lower gray matter volume in frontal, temporal, and parietal brain regions compared to healthy controls.
datoms.source: A. Lyall, L. Breithaupt, Chunni Ji, Anastasia Haidar, E. Kotler "Lower Region-Specific Gray Matter Volume in Females with Atypical Anorexia Nervosa and Anorexia Nervosa" (2024). doi:10.1002/eat.24168
datoms.population: 23 females with atypical anorexia nervosa, 41 healthy control females
datoms.measure: Gray matter volume in frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes

datoms.notes: Limitations: Not reported in the provided text.

datoms.claim: Body mass index is associated with gray matter volume in parietal, frontal, temporal, and cingulate lobes in females with eating disorders and healthy controls.
datoms.source: A. Lyall, L. Breithaupt, Chunni Ji, Anastasia Haidar, E. Kotler "Lower Region-Specific Gray Matter Volume in Females with Atypical Anorexia Nervosa and Anorexia Nervosa" (2024). doi:10.1002/eat.24168

datoms.measure: Association between BMI and gray matter volume

datoms.notes: Limitations: Not reported in the provided text.

datoms.claim: Individuals with anorexia nervosa show significantly smaller gray matter volume in multiple brain regions including the cerebellum, thalamus, temporal gyrus, orbital frontal gyrus, and sensorimotor gyrus compared to healthy controls.
datoms.source: Fengting Wang, Wei Liu, Halimureti Paerhati, Zhengyu Lin, Kuanghao Ye "Weight restoration in patients with anorexia nervosa after stereotactic surgery and brain morphometric insights" (2025). doi:10.1186/s12888-025-06890-5
datoms.population: 19 anorexia nervosa patients (6 receiving NAc DBS, 13 receiving anterior capsulotomy) and healthy controls
datoms.measure: Gray matter volume in brain regions via structural MRI
datoms.methodology: Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) structural MRI analysis
datoms.sample_size: 19 AN patients; healthy control sample size not reported
datoms.notes: Limitations: Small sample size (19 patients); further studies with larger patient numbers are warranted to better evaluate surgical outcomes and predictive value of imaging characteristics.

datoms.claim: Decreased surface area of the right inferior temporal gyrus and left lateral orbital gyrus causally decreases risk of bulimia nervosa.
datoms.source: Weihua Li, Xinghao Wang, Yiling Wang, Jiani Wang, Xinyu Huang "Dissecting the Causal Association Between Bulimia Nervosa and Structural Brain Abnormalities: A Two‐Sample Bidirectional Mendelian Randomization Study" (2025). doi:10.1002/brb3.70859
datoms.population: 2,442 individuals with genotype data from QIMR genetic epidemiology laboratory GWAS; UK Biobank structural MRI data
datoms.measure: Surface area (mm²) of right inferior temporal gyrus and left lateral orbital gyrus measured via structural MRI; odds ratio for BN risk
datoms.methodology: Two-sample bidirectional Mendelian randomization
datoms.sample_size: 2,442 participants (BN GWAS); UK Biobank 3D-T1 MRI cohort (size not specified)
datoms.notes: Limitations: Moderate GWAS sample size for BN; European genetic background limits generalizability; bidirectional causality findings may reflect shared etiological factors; gender differences and comorbid psychological symptoms not fully controlled.

datoms.claim: Individuals with anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa show bilateral reduction in cerebellar gray matter volume compared to healthy controls, with significant clusters in Crus I and Lobule VI.
datoms.source: Michelle Sader, G. Waiter, Justin H G Williams "The cerebellum plays more than one role in the dysregulation of appetite: Review of structural evidence from typical and eating disorder populations" (2023). doi:10.1002/brb3.3286
datoms.population: Individuals with anorexia nervosa (n=228) and bulimia nervosa (n=48) compared to healthy controls (n=234)
datoms.measure: Gray matter volume (GMV) in cerebellum measured via voxel-based morphometry
datoms.methodology: Systematic review and meta-analysis using GingerALE activation likelihood estimation
datoms.sample_size: 510 eating disorder participants; 787 total case-control participants
datoms.notes: Limitations: Publications older than 10 years were excluded; animal studies were excluded; only voxel-based morphometry studies were included, excluding fMRI studies; authors were unable to correct for age and gender across datasets due to limited literature.

datoms.claim: Individuals with obesity show unilateral (left hemisphere) reduction in cerebellar gray matter volume in Crus I and Lobule VI compared to healthy controls.
datoms.source: Michelle Sader, G. Waiter, Justin H G Williams "The cerebellum plays more than one role in the dysregulation of appetite: Review of structural evidence from typical and eating disorder populations" (2023). doi:10.1002/brb3.3286
datoms.population: Individuals with obesity (n=134) compared to healthy controls (n=143)
datoms.measure: Gray matter volume (GMV) in cerebellum measured via voxel-based morphometry
datoms.methodology: Systematic review and meta-analysis using GingerALE activation likelihood estimation
datoms.notes: Limitations: Publications older than 10 years were excluded; animal studies were excluded; only voxel-based morphometry studies were included, excluding fMRI studies; sensitivity analyses indicated OB-specific heterogeneity; authors were unable to correct for age and gender across datasets. Low thematic match confidence to anchor claim (similarity 0.4851823283781364).

datoms.claim: In normative populations, cerebellar gray matter volume negatively correlates with BMI in the right posterior lobe, including regions Crus I/II, Lobule VI, and Lobule VIIb.
datoms.source: Michelle Sader, G. Waiter, Justin H G Williams "The cerebellum plays more than one role in the dysregulation of appetite: Review of structural evidence from typical and eating disorder populations" (2023). doi:10.1002/brb3.3286
datoms.population: Normative/nonclinical populations across BMI spectrum (n=3830 total from 9-10 studies)
datoms.measure: Correlation between cerebellar gray matter volume and BMI via voxel-based morphometry
datoms.methodology: Systematic review and meta-analysis using GingerALE activation likelihood estimation on normative cohorts
datoms.notes: Limitations: Publications older than 10 years were excluded; animal studies were excluded; only voxel-based morphometry studies were included, excluding fMRI studies; one study (Figley et al.) did not include individuals with excess weight; three studies did not include individuals with obesity. Low thematic match confidence to anchor claim (similarity 0.3895042227698341).

datoms.claim: Individuals with anorexia nervosa show reduced brain volume detectable via MRI compared to healthy controls.
datoms.source: Linda Frintrop, Johanna Liesbrock, L. Paulukat, S. Johann, M. Kas "Reduced astrocyte density underlying brain volume reduction in activity-based anorexia rats" (2018). doi:10.1080/15622975.2016.1273552
datoms.population: Activity-based anorexia rats
datoms.measure: Brain volume reduction and astrocyte density
datoms.methodology: Animal model study with histological analysis
datoms.notes: Limitations: This is an animal model study; findings may not directly translate to human anorexia nervosa pathophysiology. The study does not directly measure human brain structure via MRI.

datoms.claim: Individuals with acute anorexia nervosa show measurable multivariate structural brain differences detectable via MRI compared to healthy controls.
datoms.source: Dominic Arold, F. Bernardoni, Daniel Geisler, Arne Doose, Volkan Uen "Predicting long-term outcome in anorexia nervosa: a machine learning analysis of brain structure at different stages of weight recovery" (2023). doi:10.1017/S0033291723001861
datoms.population: 165 acutely underweight patients with anorexia nervosa (acAN-TP1) aged 12-29 years vs. 289 healthy controls aged 12-30 years
datoms.measure: Multivariate structural brain alterations (cortical thickness and subcortical volumes) via MRI; ROC-AUC classification performance
datoms.methodology: Machine learning classification with nested cross-validation
datoms.notes: Limitations: The study included predominantly female participants (100% female) and European participants (98%), limiting generalizability. The cross-sectional design at baseline does not establish causality. The study excluded participants with bulimia nervosa history and certain medications, which may limit applicability to broader AN populations.

datoms.claim: Individuals with anorexia nervosa after partial weight restoration show measurable multivariate structural brain differences detectable via MRI compared to healthy controls.
datoms.source: Dominic Arold, F. Bernardoni, Daniel Geisler, Arne Doose, Volkan Uen "Predicting long-term outcome in anorexia nervosa: a machine learning analysis of brain structure at different stages of weight recovery" (2023). doi:10.1017/S0033291723001861
datoms.population: 115 patients with anorexia nervosa after partial weight restoration (acAN-TP2) aged 12-25 years vs. 289 healthy controls aged 12-30 years
datoms.measure: Multivariate structural brain alterations (cortical thickness and subcortical volumes) via MRI; ROC-AUC classification performance
datoms.methodology: Machine learning classification with nested cross-validation
datoms.notes: Limitations: The study included predominantly female participants (100% female) and European participants (98%). The cross-sectional design at this timepoint does not establish causality. Only 64% of acAN-TP2 participants completed the 1-year outcome assessment.

datoms.claim: Structural brain alterations in regions with high functional network centrality are more pronounced in individuals with anorexia nervosa after partial weight restoration.
datoms.source: Dominic Arold, F. Bernardoni, Daniel Geisler, Arne Doose, Volkan Uen "Predicting long-term outcome in anorexia nervosa: a machine learning analysis of brain structure at different stages of weight recovery" (2023). doi:10.1017/S0033291723001861
datoms.population: 115 patients with anorexia nervosa after partial weight restoration (acAN-TP2) aged 12-25 years; functional connectivity reference from Human Connectome Project healthy sample
datoms.measure: Correlation between cortical thickness feature importance and functional network centrality (weighted degree centrality)
datoms.methodology: Connectome contextualization using functional connectivity data from Human Connectome Project
datoms.sample_size: 115 acAN-TP2 patients; HCP reference sample (size not specified in this paper)
datoms.notes: Limitations: The analysis assumes that network centrality properties in healthy controls from the HCP also apply to individuals with AN, which may not be entirely accurate. The cross-sectional design limits causal inference about the relationship between network properties and structural alterations.

datoms.claim: Multivariate structural brain alterations in anorexia nervosa after partial weight restoration predict long-term clinical outcome at 1-year follow-up.
datoms.source: Dominic Arold, F. Bernardoni, Daniel Geisler, Arne Doose, Volkan Uen "Predicting long-term outcome in anorexia nervosa: a machine learning analysis of brain structure at different stages of weight recovery" (2023). doi:10.1017/S0033291723001861
datoms.population: 74 patients with anorexia nervosa after partial weight restoration (acAN-TP2) with complete 1-year outcome data, aged 12-25 years at baseline
datoms.measure: Morgan-Russell Outcome score at 1-year follow-up predicted by ML-based risk score derived from structural brain MRI
datoms.methodology: Generalized linear model predicting clinical outcome from ML-based risk score
datoms.sample_size: 74 acAN-TP2 patients with complete outcome data
datoms.notes: Limitations: Only 64% of acAN-TP2 participants (74 of 115) completed the structured Morgan-Russell interview at 1-year follow-up, which may introduce selection bias. The effect size is modest (R2 = 0.065), explaining only 6.5% of outcome variance. The study included predominantly female participants (100% female) and European participants (98%).

datoms.claim: Individuals with anorexia nervosa after long-term weight recovery do not show detectable multivariate structural brain differences compared to healthy controls.
datoms.source: Dominic Arold, F. Bernardoni, Daniel Geisler, Arne Doose, Volkan Uen "Predicting long-term outcome in anorexia nervosa: a machine learning analysis of brain structure at different stages of weight recovery" (2023). doi:10.1017/S0033291723001861
datoms.population: 89 long-term weight-recovered former AN patients (recAN) aged 16-30 years with at least 6 months weight recovery vs. 289 healthy controls aged 12-30 years
datoms.measure: Multivariate structural brain alterations (cortical thickness and subcortical volumes) via MRI; ROC-AUC classification performance
datoms.methodology: Machine learning classification with nested cross-validation
datoms.notes: Limitations: The study included predominantly female participants (100% female) and European participants (98%). The cross-sectional design does not establish causality. The recAN sample was older (mean age 22.18 years) than the acute AN samples, which may confound age-related brain changes. Low thematic match confidence to anchor claim (similarity 0.5047291101718451).

datoms.claim: Individuals with anorexia nervosa show reduced neuromelanin contrast-to-noise ratio in the substantia nigra pars compacta compared to healthy controls, detectable via neuromelanin-sensitive MRI.

datoms.claim: Telomere length shortening is causally associated with increased risk of anorexia nervosa through white matter microstructural changes in specific brain regions including the internal capsule, corona radiata, posterior thalamic radiation, left cingulate gyrus, left longitudinal fasciculus, and left forceps minor.
datoms.source: Haoyuan Qiu, Miao Shi, Z. Zhong, Haoran Hu, Hunini Sang "Causal Relationship between Aging and Anorexia Nervosa: A White-Matter-Microstructure-Mediated Mendelian Randomization Analysis" (2024). doi:10.3390/biomedicines12081874
datoms.population: 472,174 UK Biobank participants (telomere length); 72,517 individuals from Psychiatric Genomics Consortium (16,992 anorexia nervosa cases, 55,525 controls); 8,428 UK Biobank participants for dMRI phenotypes
datoms.measure: White matter microstructural changes (dMRI phenotypes including FA, MD, ICVF) mediating relationship between telomere length and anorexia nervosa risk
datoms.methodology: Two-step Mendelian randomization analysis with mediation effect calculation
datoms.sample_size: 472,174 participants (telomere length GWAS); 72,517 individuals (anorexia nervosa GWAS); 8,428 participants (dMRI phenotypes)
datoms.notes: Limitations: The study used GWAS summary statistics from populations of European ancestry, which may limit generalizability to other ethnic groups. The test group results showed heterogeneity, though external validation and pleiotropy analysis supported the findings. datoms.claim: Individuals with anorexia nervosa exhibit altered white matter microstructure (measured by fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity, and intracellular volume fraction) in emotion processing and cognitive control regions including the internal capsule, cingulate gyrus, and forceps minor.

datoms.measure: White matter microstructural integrity (fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity, intracellular volume fraction) in internal capsule, cingulate gyrus, and forceps minor

datoms.claim: Adolescents with anorexia nervosa show reduced fractional anisotropy (FA) in white matter regions including the corpus callosum, cingulum, and fornix compared to healthy controls in the acute disease state.

datoms.claim: White matter microstructural alterations (reduced FA and elevated mean diffusivity) in the corpus callosum, cingulum, and fornix normalize after weight restoration and psychotherapeutic treatment in adolescents with anorexia nervosa.

guide.whatScienceSays:
DATOM has linked 91 real pieces of evidence, called datoms, to this claim. Of those, 64 (70%) support the idea that people with eating disorders have measurable differences in brain structure or brain function. Another 25 (27%) partly support it, but only under specific conditions, such as one brain region, one symptom, or one subgroup of patients, rather than a clean comparison against healthy people. Just 2 (2%) argue against the claim outright.

Most of the supporting evidence points to differences in four brain areas: the insula, the prefrontal cortex, the striatum, and the cerebellum. One brain-scan study of 110 people (54 with bulimia nervosa, 56 healthy controls) found less gray matter in two insula regions tied to combining thought and emotion. Another study of 101 people (37 with anorexia nervosa, 23 with a milder form called atypical anorexia nervosa, and 41 healthy controls) linked body weight to gray matter volume across several brain regions. A separate study used a genetics-based method called Mendelian randomization to test whether bulimia nervosa actually causes these brain changes, rather than just appearing alongside them. That one study alone supplies 6 of the 91 datoms.

Together, this points to a real, if varied, pattern of brain differences in people with eating disorders. But as the next section explains, not all of that 70% support figure is built on evidence that is actually about eating disorders.
guide.howConfident:
Why doesn't 70% support add up to a high confidence score? DATOM's confidence score for this claim is just 35%, in the Preliminary band, even though 64 of 91 datoms (70%) support the claim and only 2 (2%) go against it. That gap exists because DATOM's confidence score is not a vote count. It weighs how relevant and how solid the evidence actually is, not just which way it leans.

Start with relevance. Nearly half the evidence, 44 of the 91 datoms (48%), was flagged by DATOM's own matching system as a weak topic match. When we manually checked those 44, about 34 of them turned out not to be about eating disorders at all. They covered brain inflammation linked to a skin condition called atopic dermatitis, brain connectivity in tobacco use, borderline personality disorder, ADHD, moral decision making, brainwave patterns in sleepy shift workers, and memory tests in rats. Those studies were pulled into the corpus because of similar language, not because they are actually about eating disorders. So a real chunk of the 70% support figure rests on evidence that is not on topic.

Then there is the quality of what is left. 40 of the 91 datoms (44%) come from thin text summaries rather than the full original research paper, so there is less detail to check them against. 24 of the 91 (26%) do not say how many people or samples the study used at all. Among the 66 datoms that do report a sample size, DATOM's own scoring flags 31 of them (47%) as too small a group to trust the result strongly.

Finally, this evidence base is narrower than it looks. All 91 datoms trace back to just 40 separate research papers, and the single biggest contributor, the Mendelian randomization study mentioned above, supplies 6 of the 91 by itself. Add up the weak relevance, the thin sourcing, and the narrow set of underlying papers, and you can see why DATOM does not treat 70% support as anything close to settled science.
decisionSupport: The overall pattern (70% support, 2% against, out of 91 pieces of evidence) lines up with real, repeated findings of brain differences in the insula, prefrontal cortex, striatum, and cerebellum, including less gray matter in the anterior insula found in a 110-person study comparing 54 people with bulimia nervosa to 56 healthy people.

Before treating this as decision-grade evidence, set aside the 44 of 91 datoms (48%) flagged as a weak topic match. On inspection, roughly 34 of them describe people or animals with no eating disorder diagnosis at all, such as skin conditions (atopic dermatitis), tobacco use, ADHD, borderline personality disorder, animal studies in rodents, and shift workers' brainwave patterns. So the real support rate for evidence that is actually about eating disorders is meaningfully lower than the raw 70%.

Treat sample size claims with caution. 24 of the 91 datoms (26%) do not report how many people were studied at all, and among the 66 that do, DATOM's own scoring flags 31 of them (47%) as too small a group to trust the result strongly.

Very little evidence directly disagrees with the claim, just 2 of 91 datoms (2%). So the real question is not support versus opposition, it is how much of the evidence is actually relevant versus loosely matched, and how much weight to give evidence that traces back to only 40 separate research papers rather than 91 independent studies.

Most of this evidence is recent: 66 of the 91 datoms (73%) come from 2024 to 2026. Only 10 of the 91 are the kind of study that combines many other studies together (meta-analyses or systematic reviews). Most of the rest are single, individual findings, several pulled from the same paper, that have not yet been confirmed by independent researchers.
guide.faultLines:
The Topic Match Is Often Loose: 44 of the 91 datoms (48%) were flagged by DATOM's own matching system as a weak topic match to this claim, and that is not a small technical detail. When we manually checked those 44, about 34 of them turned out to describe people, or in some cases rats, with no eating disorder diagnosis at all: brain inflammation linked to a skin condition called atopic dermatitis, brain connectivity in tobacco use, borderline personality disorder, ADHD, moral decision making, brainwave patterns in sleepy shift workers, and memory tests in rats. A real chunk of the 70% support figure rests on evidence that is only loosely related to eating disorders, not direct proof of the claim.

Missing Details on the Studies: 40 of the 91 datoms (44%) come from thin text summaries instead of the full original research paper, and 24 of the 91 (26%) do not say how many people or samples were studied at all. Among the 66 datoms that do report a sample size, DATOM's own scoring flags 31 of them (47%) as too small a group to trust the result strongly. A large share of this evidence base cannot currently be checked for basic reliability before it gets counted toward the 70% figure.

Same Handful of Papers, Counted Many Times: the 91 datoms actually trace back to only 40 separate research papers, spread across roughly 18 institutions, and 23 of those papers each contributed more than one datom. The single biggest contributor, a Mendelian randomization study on bulimia nervosa, supplies 6 of the 91 by itself. Counting every extracted finding as its own separate piece of evidence makes the evidence base look broader than it really is, since it comes from a smaller set of underlying research groups.

No Two Studies Did It the Same Way: the 91 datoms use 72 different research methods between them, most used only once or twice. These range from brain scans that measure volume, to brain scans that track activity while people rest, to 8 datoms using Mendelian randomization (a genetics-based method for testing cause and effect), to 10 that combine multiple studies together. Averaging all of these into one number hides real differences between them, especially the gap between studies that just find a correlation and the smaller group that actually tests whether brain differences cause disordered eating, are caused by it, or simply happen alongside it.

name: Structural Brain Alterations in Eating Disorders
plainQuestion: Do brain scans (MRI/fMRI) show measurable structural or functional differences in people with eating disorders compared to people without them?
scope: This claim is about teenagers and adults with anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating, or a clinically significant risk of an eating disorder, compared to healthy people without one. About a third of the 91 linked datoms actually describe people or animals outside that group, for example people with atopic dermatitis, ADHD, or tobacco use, or lab rodents, because of loose topic matching.
metric: What is measured: the amount of gray matter (the brain's processing tissue), the thickness of the brain's outer layer, the structure of the brain's white matter wiring (measured with scan techniques called DTI or fixel-based analysis), and brain activity and connectivity seen on functional MRI scans, whether at rest or during a task, in areas including the insula, prefrontal cortex, striatum, and cerebellum.
aboutClaim: This claim is built on 91 pieces of evidence. 64 of them (70%) support the idea that eating disorders come with measurable brain differences, and only 2 (2%) argue against it. But DATOM's confidence score for this claim is just 35%, in the Preliminary band. Why the gap? Nearly half the evidence, 44 of 91 (48%), was flagged by DATOM's matching system as a weak topic match, and a manual check found about 34 of those are really about unrelated things like skin conditions, ADHD, or fear-response tests in rats, not eating disorder patients. On top of that, 40 of 91 (44%) come from thin text summaries rather than full research papers, 24 do not report how many people were studied, and all 91 pieces of evidence trace back to only 40 separate research papers. The strong-looking 70% support figure comes with real caveats about relevance, missing details, and how narrow the underlying research actually is.
